--- title: "Cross-validation" description: "Five or ten folds of sites are enough, and their out-of-fold predictions are pooled into one score. When the same folds also choose the model, the winner's score is too good; nested cross-validation scores the choosing as well." order: 1 categories: [validation] --- ## The folds that choose a model cannot also score it [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) chose a tree's node size by cross-validation by site, and noted that the winner's error was a little flattering, being the lowest of 12. With 12 candidates the flattery is small. With a hundred, it can make a model padded with pure noise look like the best on offer. This page shows how to report a cross-validated score honestly: how many folds to use, how to turn them into one number, and how to score a model when the same folds also chose it. The last matters most when a survey is too small to set test sites aside, which is common in marine work. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Out-of-fold predictions are pooled into one score In cross-validation each station is predicted once, by the model fitted without its site. That prediction is the station's **out-of-fold prediction**. Pooling the out-of-fold predictions of every station and working out one RMSE from them gives the **pooled score**. `collect_metrics()` in tidymodels reports something slightly different: the average of the folds' own RMSEs, which [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) used. The two agree when the folds are few and large. With many small folds they part, because a large miss raises only its own fold's RMSE, and the average gives that fold the same weight as every quiet one. Pooling has a second use. Any scheme that holds out every station once scores the same stations, so pooled scores from different schemes can be compared. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) relies on this. ## Nested cross-validation scores the search as well Choosing among candidates is part of building a model, whether the candidates are settings, sets of inputs or methods. A search scores every candidate by cross-validation and keeps the lowest. But each score is partly luck: these folds happen to suit some candidates more than others. The lowest of many scores gathers the most luck, so the more candidates there are, the more the winner's score flatters it. This is **selection optimism**. **Nested cross-validation** measures what the whole search is worth. An outer cross-validation holds out one fold of sites at a time. Inside each outer round the search runs in full on the remaining sites, with inner folds of its own, and chooses a candidate. The chosen candidate is fitted to those sites and scored on the outer fold, which played no part in the choice. The outer folds' predictions, pooled, score the search: how well a model chosen this way predicts new sites. ::: {.diagram} ![Nested cross-validation. In each outer round, one fold of sites is held out and the search runs on the rest, scoring every candidate on inner folds of its own. The candidate it chooses is fitted to those sites and predicts the outer fold once. The outer folds' predictions, pooled into one score, score the search.](img/nested-cross-validation.svg){fig-alt="In outer round 1 of 5, the first of five folds of sites is held out and the other four are handed to the search. The search cuts those four folds into inner folds; in each inner round one inner fold is held out and every candidate is scored on it. The candidate with the lowest inner error is chosen, fitted to all four folds and used once to predict the outer fold. Three steps follow: repeat for each of the five outer folds; pool the outer folds' predictions into one score; that score is the search's, choice included. A note says the outer fold plays no part in the choice, so its error is not flattered by it."} ::: A search therefore produces three things that are easy to confuse. The winner's cross-validated score tells you which candidate to keep. The nested score is the one to report. The final model, the winner refitted to all the data, has no score of its own: the nested score is the best guess at how it will do on new sites. ## Worked example The model is Poisson regression from [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd), with each input entered as a straight line. Nested cross-validation needs no test sites, so this page uses all the survey's sites. Every fold holds whole sites, as in [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd). ### Preparing the data `fit_resamples()` fits a workflow in every round of the folds, and with `save_pred = TRUE` it keeps the out-of-fold predictions; `collect_predictions()` gathers them, one per station. In scikit-learn, `cross_val_predict()` does both. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") # Poisson regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round poisson_on <- function(vars, data) { recipe(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = data) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> workflow(poisson_reg()) } cross_validate <- function(vars, data, folds) { fit_resamples(poisson_on(vars, data), folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) } # one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction pooled_rmse <- function(rounds) { collect_predictions(rounds) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> pull(.estimate) } tibble(stations = nrow(survey), sites = n_distinct(survey$site_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| sites| |--------:|-----:| | 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, LeaveOneGroupOut, cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() sites = survey["site_id"] inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] # Poisson regression on any set of inputs, with gaps filled inside each round def poisson_on(columns): numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical] nominal = [c for c in columns if c in categorical] steps = [ # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric), ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), nominal), ] # a candidate may have no numeric or no categorical inputs recipe = ColumnTransformer([step for step in steps if step[2]]) return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000))]) # one RMSE from every station's out-of-fold prediction def pooled_rmse(columns, data, folds, groups): predicted = cross_val_predict(poisson_on(columns), data[columns], data["abundance"], cv=folds, groups=groups) return root_mean_squared_error(data["abundance"], predicted) pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)], "sites": [sites.nunique()]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | sites | |-----------:|--------:| | 800 | 160 | ::: ::: ::: ### Five or ten folds are enough The eight inputs are cross-validated with 2, 5, 10 and 20 folds of sites, each ten times with the sites dealt into new folds, and once with every site a fold of its own (**leave-one-site-out**, 160 folds). Each run gives the pooled score and the average of the folds' RMSEs. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) sweep <- map(c(2, 5, 10, 20), \(v) { map(1:10, \(r) { rounds <- cross_validate(inputs, survey, group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = v)) tibble(folds = v, pooled = pooled_rmse(rounds), averaged = collect_metrics(rounds)$mean) }) |> list_rbind() }) |> list_rbind() # v = NULL makes one fold per site one_site <- cross_validate(inputs, survey, group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id)) sweep <- bind_rows(sweep, tibble(folds = n_sites, pooled = pooled_rmse(one_site), averaged = collect_metrics(one_site)$mean)) sweep |> summarise(`pooled RMSE` = mean(pooled), `average of the folds' RMSEs` = mean(averaged), .by = folds) |> mutate(across(-folds, \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| folds| pooled RMSE| average of the folds' RMSEs| |-----:|-----------:|---------------------------:| | 2| 4.43| 4.42| | 5| 4.37| 4.33| | 10| 4.34| 4.27| | 20| 4.35| 4.24| | 160| 4.37| 3.83|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} observed = survey["abundance"].to_numpy() def pooled_and_averaged(folds): predicted = np.empty(len(survey)) fold_rmse = [] for fit_rows, new_rows in folds.split(survey, groups=sites): fitted = poisson_on(inputs).fit(survey.iloc[fit_rows][inputs], observed[fit_rows]) predicted[new_rows] = fitted.predict(survey.iloc[new_rows][inputs]) fold_rmse.append(root_mean_squared_error(observed[new_rows], predicted[new_rows])) return {"pooled": root_mean_squared_error(observed, predicted), "averaged": np.mean(fold_rmse)} runs = [{"folds": v, **pooled_and_averaged(GroupKFold(n_splits=v, shuffle=True, random_state=r))} for v in (2, 5, 10, 20) for r in range(10)] runs.append({"folds": sites.nunique(), **pooled_and_averaged(LeaveOneGroupOut())}) (pd.DataFrame(runs) .groupby("folds") .agg(**{"pooled RMSE": ("pooled", "mean"), "average of the folds' RMSEs": ("averaged", "mean")}) .reset_index() .round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | folds | pooled RMSE | average of the folds' RMSEs | |--------:|--------------:|------------------------------:| | 2 | 4.38 | 4.37 | | 5 | 4.37 | 4.34 | | 10 | 4.37 | 4.31 | | 20 | 4.37 | 4.26 | | 160 | 4.37 | 3.83 | ::: ::: ::: **Two folds are a little pessimistic.** Each round fits to half the sites, and a model fitted to half the data predicts worse than one fitted to most of it: its pooled RMSE is 4.43. From five folds on, the pooled score barely moves: 4.37 with five folds, 4.34 with ten, 4.35 with twenty and 4.37 with every site on its own. More folds only add fitting. Five or ten folds are the usual choice, and ten is cheap at this size. **The average of the folds' RMSEs drifts down as the folds get smaller,** from 4.42 with two folds to 3.83 with one site per fold, 0.54 below the pooled score. The model did not change; only the bookkeeping did. A score that depends on the number of folds cannot be compared across studies, which is why the rest of this section pools. ### A search over 100 sets of inputs picks noise Twenty columns of random numbers, `noise_1` to `noise_20`, are added to the survey. They carry no information about the catch. A search then draws 100 candidates, each Poisson regression on five of the 28 columns, and scores every candidate by ten-fold cross-validation by site. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(21) noise <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(survey) * 20), ncol = 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise_", 1:20))) noisy <- bind_cols(survey, as_tibble(noise)) columns <- c(inputs, colnames(noise)) candidates <- map(1:100, \(i) sample(columns, 5)) folds <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 10) searched <- map_dbl(candidates, \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, noisy, folds))) winner <- candidates[[which.min(searched)]] tibble(best = min(searched), median = median(searched), worst = max(searched)) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| best| median| worst| |----:|------:|-----:| | 4.5| 4.73| 4.92|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} winner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "longitude" "noise_13" "season" "noise_17" "substrate" ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(21) noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(survey), 20)), columns=[f"noise_{i}" for i in range(1, 21)]) noisy = pd.concat([survey, noise], axis=1) columns = inputs + list(noise.columns) candidates = [[str(c) for c in rng.choice(columns, 5, replace=False)] for i in range(100)] folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=21) searched = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, noisy, folds, sites) for c in candidates]) winner = candidates[searched.argmin()] print(pd.DataFrame({"best": [searched.min()], "median": [np.median(searched)], "worst": [searched.max()]}).round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> best median worst #> 0 4.48 4.7 4.81 ``` ::: ```{.python .cell-code} winner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> ['longitude', 'noise_13', 'substrate', 'noise_3', 'chlorophyll_mg_m3'] ``` ::: ::: ::: The winner scores 4.50, the lowest of the 100, and two of its five columns are noise. Its real inputs, `longitude`, `season` and `substrate`, carry what skill it has; the noise columns ride along because they happened to suit these folds. A study that searched this way would report 4.50 as the model's error on new sites. ### Nested cross-validation shows what the search is worth The search is now run inside an outer five-fold cross-validation by site, with five inner folds. For comparison, Poisson regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, is fitted and scored on the same outer folds. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(32) outer <- group_vfold_cv(noisy, group = site_id, v = 5) nested <- map(outer$splits, \(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) held <- assessment(s) inner <- group_vfold_cv(fitting, group = site_id, v = 5) inner_rmse <- map_dbl(candidates, \(vars) pooled_rmse(cross_validate(vars, fitting, inner))) chosen <- candidates[[which.min(inner_rmse)]] predict_held <- function(vars) { predict(fit(poisson_on(vars, fitting), fitting), held)$.pred } tibble(abundance = held$abundance, claimed = min(inner_rmse), searched = predict_held(chosen), eight_inputs = predict_held(inputs), noise_chosen = sum(str_starts(chosen, "noise"))) }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "outer_fold") nested |> summarise(`search claimed` = first(claimed), `search's choice, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, searched), `eight inputs, outer fold` = rmse_vec(abundance, eight_inputs), `noise columns chosen` = first(noise_chosen), .by = outer_fold) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| outer_fold| search claimed| search's choice, outer fold| eight inputs, outer fold| noise columns chosen| |----------:|--------------:|---------------------------:|------------------------:|--------------------:| | 1| 4.72| 3.57| 3.33| 2| | 2| 4.23| 5.35| 4.89| 2| | 3| 4.59| 4.10| 3.91| 2| | 4| 4.19| 6.33| 5.30| 2| | 5| 4.35| 4.56| 4.20| 2|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} outer = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=32) rounds = [] for k, (fit_rows, held_rows) in enumerate(outer.split(noisy, groups=sites), start=1): fitting, held = noisy.iloc[fit_rows], noisy.iloc[held_rows] inner = GroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=k) inner_rmse = np.array([pooled_rmse(c, fitting, inner, fitting["site_id"]) for c in candidates]) chosen = candidates[inner_rmse.argmin()] def predict_held(columns): fitted = poisson_on(columns).fit(fitting[columns], fitting["abundance"]) return fitted.predict(held[columns]) rounds.append(pd.DataFrame({ "outer_fold": k, "abundance": held["abundance"].to_numpy(), "claimed": inner_rmse.min(), "searched": predict_held(chosen), "eight_inputs": predict_held(inputs), "noise_chosen": sum(c.startswith("noise") for c in chosen)})) nested = pd.concat(rounds, ignore_index=True) (nested.groupby("outer_fold") .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "search claimed": g["claimed"].iloc[0], "search's choice, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["searched"]), "eight inputs, outer fold": root_mean_squared_error(g["abundance"], g["eight_inputs"]), "noise columns chosen": g["noise_chosen"].iloc[0]}), include_groups=False) .reset_index() .round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | outer_fold | search claimed | search's choice, outer fold | eight inputs, outer fold | noise columns chosen | |-------------:|-----------------:|------------------------------:|---------------------------:|-----------------------:| | 1 | 4.63 | 3.95 | 3.75 | 2 | | 2 | 4.27 | 5.3 | 4.99 | 3 | | 3 | 4.4 | 4.52 | 4.35 | 2 | | 4 | 4.48 | 4.26 | 4.02 | 2 | | 5 | 4.64 | 4.21 | 4.07 | 2 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} per_fold |> pivot_longer(c(claimed, searched, eight), names_to = "score", values_to = "rmse") |> mutate(score = factor(score, c("claimed", "searched", "eight"), c("Search claimed", "Search's choice on the outer fold", "Eight inputs, no search, on the outer fold")), outer_fold = factor(outer_fold, 5:1)) |> ggplot(aes(rmse, outer_fold)) + geom_line(aes(group = outer_fold), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_point(aes(colour = score, shape = score), size = 3.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("grey", "vermilion", "blue")])) + scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16, 16)) + labs(x = "RMSE (individuals)", y = "Outer fold", colour = NULL, shape = NULL, title = "Eight inputs with no search beat the search's choice") + guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each outer fold of the nested cross-validation: the error the search claimed for its choice on the inner folds, the error of that choice on the outer fold, and the error of Poisson regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search, on the same outer fold.](cross-validation_files/figure-html/fig-nested-1.png){#fig-nested fig-alt='A dot plot with the five outer folds down the side and RMSE in individuals along the bottom. Each fold has three points. The search\'s claimed errors average 4.42. On the outer folds the search\'s choice lands to the right of its claim in 3 of the five folds, and the model on the eight inputs lands to the left of the search\'s choice in all five.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The search claimed an average error of 4.42 on its inner folds. Pooled over the outer folds, the models it chose score **4.86**: that is the nested score, 0.44 worse than claimed, and the honest figure for a model found by this search. In every outer round, two of the five columns it chose were noise. On a single outer fold the choice can do better than claimed, because some folds hold sites that are easier to predict; pooled over all five, it does worse. Poisson regression on the eight measured inputs, with no search at all, scores 4.37 on the same outer folds, and beats the search's choice in all five. The search did not find a better model; it found the candidates that suited its folds best. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Each station's **out-of-fold prediction** comes from the model fitted without its site. The **pooled score** is one RMSE over all of them; unlike the average of the folds' RMSEs, it does not drift with the number of folds. - **Five or ten folds are enough.** Two fit to too little of the data; more than ten only add fitting. - The winner of a search has the lowest of many scores, and part of its lead is luck: **selection optimism**. Here a search over 100 sets of inputs chose noise columns and claimed 4.42. - **Nested cross-validation** runs the whole search inside each outer round and scores its choice on the outer fold. It put the search at 4.86, behind the eight measured inputs with no search (4.37). - Report the nested score, not the winner's. The final model, refitted to all the data, has no score of its own. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add the eight measured inputs to the candidates as a 101st set. Does the search choose it, and how far does the nested score move? 2. Draw 1,000 candidates instead of 100. Does the winner's claimed score fall, and does the nested score follow it?
